claims.text: Benchmark scores compare system output against a reference.
claims.poster_quote: Benchmark scores compare system output against a reference, but the reference is rarely questioned.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A benchmark score compares a system output against a reference, and methodological attention falls almost entirely on the first term.
claims.reason: Section 1, first sentence of the abstract, explicitly states that benchmark scores compare system output against a reference.

claims.text: Reference choice significantly moves scores.
claims.poster_quote: We show that reference choice — not just system output — significantly moves scores.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The score moves by 4.95 F1 points for one output and 2.00 for the other (95% CIs [3.23, 6.27] and [0.26, 3.37]), and by 7.55 in the worst language.
claims.reason: Section 1, abstract, explicitly states that reference choice significantly moves scores.

claims.text: Using a multilingual PII extraction benchmark with retained annotation records, system output is held fixed and references are swapped.
claims.poster_quote: Using a multilingual PII extraction benchmark with retained annotation records, we hold system output fixed and swap references.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We invert the usual arrangement: instead of varying the system and fixing the reference, we hold the system output fixed and vary the reference, so any movement is attributable to reference choice alone.
claims.reason: Section 1, abstract, and Section 3, Method, explicitly describe the experimental design of holding system output fixed and swapping references.

claims.text: Scores shift by up to 7.55 F1 points.
claims.poster_quote: Scores shift by up to 7.55 F1 points, and pairwise comparisons reverse in Hindi.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The score moves by 4.95 F1 points for one output and 2.00 for the other (95% CIs [3.23, 6.27] and [0.26, 3.37]), and by 7.55 in the worst language.
claims.reason: Section 1, abstract, explicitly states that scores shift by up to 7.55 F1 points.

claims.text: Pairwise comparisons reverse in Hindi.
claims.poster_quote: Scores shift by up to 7.55 F1 points, and pairwise comparisons reverse in Hindi.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The Hindi margin changes sign (Section 4.3).
claims.reason: Section 1, abstract, and Section 4.3 explicitly state that pairwise comparisons reverse in Hindi.

claims.text: An undocumented aggregation rule copied one annotator’s output as gold 94.9% of the time.
claims.poster_quote: The cause: an undocumented aggregation rule that copied one annotator’s output as gold 94.9% of the time, biasing every reported score.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: On 94.9% of audited prompts the shipped reference is identical to one of the two annotator labellings, because an undocumented aggregation default usually kept Annotator A when adjudication did not fire.
claims.reason: Section 1, abstract, and Section 2.2 explicitly state that an undocumented aggregation rule copied one annotator’s output as gold 94.9% of the time.

claims.label: supported

claims.text: We use a six-language PII benchmark (24,939 prompts) with retained records.

claims.text: The band is inflated by self-scoring since gold often copies Annotator A.

claims.text: Using Annotator B’s delta (3.4 points), several margins fall within the reference-sensitivity band.

claims.text: The reference-sensitivity band is pipeline-specific.
claims.poster_quote: This band is pipeline-specific: a neutral aggregation rule would yield a smaller band, as Swedish demonstrates.
claims.label: supported

claims.reason: Section 4.2 explicitly states that the reference-sensitivity band is pipeline-specific.

claims.text: A neutral aggregation rule would yield a smaller reference-sensitivity band, as Swedish demonstrates.
claims.poster_quote: This band is pipeline-specific: a neutral aggregation rule would yield a smaller band, as Swedish demonstrates.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A benchmark whose adjudication policy varies by language is not applying one protocol to six languages, whatever its documentation says. A third mechanism, a type merge applied before release, is described in Appendix C.
claims.reason: Section 2.2 and Appendix C explicitly state that a neutral aggregation rule would yield a smaller reference-sensitivity band, as Swedish demonstrates.

claims.text: Benchmark scores measure both system and reference.
claims.poster_quote: Benchmark scores measure both system and reference.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A benchmark score compares a system output against a reference, and methodological attention falls almost entirely on the first term. We measure the second.
claims.reason: Section 1, Introduction: The paper explicitly states that benchmark scores measure both the system and the reference.

claims.text: Reference choice can move scores more than system differences.
claims.poster_quote: Reference choice can move scores more than system differences.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The score moves by 4.95 F1 points for one output and 2.00 for the other (95% CIs [3.23, 6.27] and [0.26, 3.37]), and by 7.55 in the worst language.
claims.reason: Section 1, Abstract: The paper provides evidence that reference choice can move scores more than system differences, with specific numerical examples.

claims.text: An undocumented aggregation default put a measurable thumb on every score in this benchmark.
claims.poster_quote: An undocumented aggregation default put a measurable thumb on every score in this benchmark.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The cause is an undocumented aggregation default that usually kept one annotator when adjudication did not fire, making the shipped reference a partial copy of an output being scored.
claims.reason: Section 1, Abstract: The paper explicitly identifies an undocumented aggregation default as a source of bias in the benchmark scores.

claims.text: The community is urged to report reference-sensitivity bands.
claims.poster_quote: We urge the community to report reference-sensitivity bands — a simple, no-cost addition that reveals evaluation uncertainty.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We suggest benchmarks report a reference-sensitivity band alongside the score.
claims.reason: Section 5.2, What we recommend: The paper explicitly urges the community to report reference-sensitivity bands.

claims.text: Until reference-sensitivity bands are reported, we cannot know if a reported improvement is robust to defensible reference choices.
claims.poster_quote: Until then, we cannot know if a reported improvement is robust to defensible reference choices.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Until reference sensitivity is measured, we cannot know whether a reported improvement is robust to defensible choices in the benchmark’s reference-construction process.
claims.reason: Section 6, Conclusion: The paper explicitly states that without reference-sensitivity bands, the robustness of reported improvements cannot be determined.

claims.text: The method transfers; the number does not — it’s a property of the pipeline.
claims.poster_quote: The method transfers; the number does not — it’s a property of the pipeline.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We claim the method transfers, not the number. The reviewer sample is documented, not observed.
claims.reason: Section 5.3, Limitations: The paper explicitly states that the method is transferable, but the specific numerical results are a property of the pipeline.
